0.title: Two Books, One Author
0.essay:
Many people assume that faith and science are old enemies, and that a thinking person must sooner or later choose between them. Christians have usually seen it differently. The God who gave us the Bible also made the world that scientists study, and both speak of him.

Real questions

That does not make the questions easy. How old is the earth? What should we make of evolution? Was Adam a real man? Can someone who understands the laws of nature believe in miracles? Can science explain everything, or are there questions it cannot reach? These are not idle puzzles. Students meet them in lectures, and some young people drift from the faith because no one helped them think them through.

Honest and unafraid

This study tries to take those questions seriously. It aims to describe the science accurately, to set out the main Christian views fairly, and to state this commentary’s own convictions plainly, including where they stand against the present scientific consensus. Christians have nothing to gain from caricature, and nothing to fear from the truth. “Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them” (Psalm 111:2).

Above all, it keeps Christ at the centre. The world was made through him, it holds together in him, and it will be made new by him. The scientist in the laboratory and the believer with an open Bible are looking at the work of the same Lord.

The study Creation & the Fall expounds Genesis 1 to 3, and Apologetics sets out the case for God and the resurrection. This study looks at where those subjects meet the sciences.

The chapters

God’s Two Books; Where Modern Science Grew; The Days of Genesis and the Age of the Earth; Evolution and the First Adam; Miracles and the Laws of Nature; and The Limits of Science, and Honest Conversations.

For reflection

Which question about faith and science troubles you most, or troubles someone you love? Bring it honestly to God, and ask him for both courage and humility as you read.

1.title: God’s Two Books
1.essay:
Christians have long said that God speaks in two ways: in the world he made and in the word he gave. Both come from the same God, so in the end they cannot disagree. But we can misread either one, and much of the trouble between faith and science begins there.

The book of creation

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge” (Psalm 19:1–2). Paul says that God’s “eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made” (Romans 1:20). Theologians call this general revelation: what God shows of himself to everyone, everywhere, through what he has made.

The Belgic Confession (1561) pictures creation as a beautifully written book, in which every creature, great and small, is like a letter leading us to see the invisible things of God. The study Apologetics explores how creation points to its Maker; here we ask how studying creation relates to reading Scripture.

The book of Scripture

Creation tells us that God is, and that he is mighty and wise. It cannot tell us his name, his promises, or how a sinner can be forgiven. For that he gave his word. The same psalm that hears the skies speaking turns to Scripture: “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7). The Belgic Confession adds that God makes himself known more clearly and fully in his word. Creation speaks without words (Psalm 19:3); in Scripture God speaks in sentences. So Scripture is the clearer book, and it is our final authority.

Why they cannot truly contradict

Both books have one Author. “All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). The Son who is the living Word “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). God does not lie in his word, and he does not mislead in his works. So where the two seem to clash, the fault lies in a reader, not in either book. All truth is God’s truth.

Readers can err

That calls for humility on both sides. Scientists can misread the world. Theories that once seemed certain have been revised or overturned, and good science expects to be corrected. Bible readers can misread Scripture too.

The psalmist sings that “the world is established; it shall never be moved” (Psalm 93:1). For centuries many took such verses to teach that the earth stands still at the centre of the universe. When Copernicus and later Galileo argued that the earth moves round the sun, some churchmen, Protestant as well as Catholic, objected on biblical grounds, and in 1633 the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo. The real story is more tangled than the legend. Many leading astronomers of the day also rejected the moving earth, the evidence for it was then incomplete, and politics and personalities played their part. But the reading of the psalm was mistaken. It speaks of the stability God gives his world under his reign, not of planetary motion, just as we still speak of sunrise without denying astronomy. Galileo, himself a Catholic believer, argued that Scripture and nature cannot disagree, because both come from God.

Two errors to avoid

One error makes science the master of Scripture: whatever the latest consensus says, the Bible must be bent to fit. But theories change, and God’s word stands. The opposite error treats our own reading of Scripture as infallible and refuses ever to learn from the study of nature. Augustine, writing on Genesis some sixteen centuries ago, warned Christians against speaking confidently and ignorantly about the natural world in front of unbelievers who knew better, because it brought Scripture itself into contempt.

Scripture alone is our final authority, and its plain meaning is to be followed. But when careful study of creation raises a question, it may rightly send us back to the text to ask whether we have read it well, as the Galileo affair did. Sometimes we find the text says exactly what we thought, and we hold firm and wait. Sometimes we find we had read into it what was never there. The task needs both reverence and honesty.

Studying as worship

A geology student went to her pastor troubled. Her lectures and her Bible seemed to pull in different directions. He did not tell her to drop either. He reminded her that God wrote both books, that she could study rocks to his glory, and that some questions would need patience. They read Psalm 19 together, and she went back to her lectures as a worshipper rather than a spy.

“Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them” (Psalm 111:2). To study creation is to trace the handiwork of Christ, in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). And the same Lord who set the stars in place has spoken to us in his word, and supremely in his Son.

For reflection

Why can God’s works and God’s word never truly contradict? What does the Galileo affair teach about misreading Scripture? Which error are you more prone to: letting the latest theory rule the Bible, or refusing ever to learn from creation? How might Psalm 19 change the way you look at the night sky or a science textbook?

2.title: Where Modern Science Grew
2.essay:
A popular story says that science and Christianity have always been at war. Historians of science tell a different and more interesting story, though it must be told without overclaiming.

The warfare myth

The idea of a long war between science and religion was popularised in the late nineteenth century, above all by two books, by John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White. Most historians of science now regard it as a myth, or at best a great oversimplification. Its claim that medieval Christians thought the earth was flat is false: educated people in the Middle Ages knew it is a sphere. There have been real conflicts, such as the Galileo affair, but they are not the whole story, nor even its main thread.

Many roots

Greek thinkers laid foundations in mathematics and astronomy. Scholars in the medieval Islamic world made major advances in optics, medicine and algebra. India and China made discoveries too. No single faith or culture owns science.

Yet the sustained, experimental science that took shape in Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries grew in soil shaped by the Christian doctrine of creation. Historians debate how much weight to give this, but several convictions helped.

Convictions that helped

The world is orderly. It was made by one wise God, not a quarrelling crowd of gods, and he rules it by what Jeremiah calls “the fixed order of heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 33:25). So there was reason to look for laws.

The world is contingent. God was free to make it as he pleased, so we cannot work out how it is by reasoning in an armchair. We have to go and look. Observation and experiment suit a world that was freely created.

The world is good, and it is not God. Matter is not evil, so it is worth studying. Nature is not divine, so it may be measured and examined without irreverence.

Our minds bear God’s image. “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27), so there is reason to expect human thought to fit the world. And the call to “fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28) gave study of nature a purpose: medicine and invention could be ways of loving our neighbour. Francis Bacon urged his readers to study both the book of God’s word and the book of God’s works, and hoped that learning would relieve human hardship.

Scientists of faith

Many pioneers of modern science were sincere believers, though we must not turn them into something they were not. Johannes Kepler, a Lutheran, saw his astronomy as tracing the Creator’s design. Robert Boyle, a founder of modern chemistry, wrote on theology and left money in his will for lectures defending the Christian faith. Isaac Newton wrote more on theology than on physics and believed the ordered heavens showed a wise Creator, though in private he rejected the doctrine of the Trinity.

Michael Faraday, who discovered electromagnetic induction, served as an elder in a small Christian church. James Clerk Maxwell, whose equations united electricity and magnetism, was a devout Christian, and the words of Psalm 111:2 were carved in Latin over the door of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, where he was the first professor. Gregor Mendel, whose work on peas founded genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian Catholic priest, was among the first to propose that the universe is expanding, and suggested that it began from an extremely dense early state.

Many scientists today are Christians, among them Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project. Belief is less common among scientists than in the wider population, especially among leading researchers, and Christians in the sciences hold differing views on the questions that follow in this study. But faith and first-rate science have lived together in a great many minds.

Careful, not proud

We must not overclaim. Christianity did not produce science single-handed, some believers have opposed good science, and a famous scientist’s faith does not prove Christianity true. The point is more modest, but it matters: there is no built-in war. The Christian doctrine of creation gave strong reasons to expect the world to be intelligible and worth exploring.

A young researcher was the only Christian in her laboratory. A colleague assumed that faith must make her suspicious of science. Over coffee she explained that she loved her work because she believed the world was ordered, having been made, and she wanted to understand what God had done. They kept talking for months.

Christ at the centre

“For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible… And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17). The order that every experiment relies on is not a bare fact that explains itself. It is the steady faithfulness of the Son who holds all things together. The hands that hold the galaxies were stretched out on a cross for sinners. When a scientist catches his breath at an elegant equation, he is, whether he knows it or not, echoing the psalmist: “O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all” (Psalm 104:24).

For reflection

Why do most historians reject the idea of a constant war between science and Christianity? Which Christian convictions helped science to grow, and why? How can we honour Christian scientists of the past without overclaiming? How does Colossians 1:16–17 change the way you think about the laws of nature?

3.title: The Days of Genesis and the Age of the Earth
3.essay:
How old is the earth, and how should we read the six days of Genesis 1? The study Creation & the Fall works through the text; here we set the main readings beside the sciences, and ask how to hold this commentary’s view with both conviction and honesty.

What the sciences say

The mainstream scientific estimate is that the universe is about 13.8 billion years old and the earth about 4.5 billion. These figures do not rest on one method. Radioactive dating of rocks and meteorites, the layers of sedimentary rock, ice cores, light from distant galaxies and the faint radiation left over from the early universe point, by largely independent routes, to a very old earth and an older universe. Most geologists and astronomers regard this as among the most secure conclusions in their fields, and many Christians in those fields accept it.

The main Christian views

Christians who hold Scripture to be God’s word read Genesis 1 in several ways. The young-earth view reads the days as six ordinary days, and the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 as history, so that creation is thousands rather than billions of years old. Its holders explain much of the evidence for long ages by the uniqueness of the creation week and, often, by the flood.

The day-age view, held by many progressive creationists, takes each day as a long age and matches the order of the days to the scientific timescale.

The framework view sees the days as a literary structure, with realms formed on days one to three and filled on days four to six, arranged by theme rather than by time. The analogical view sees them as God’s work-days, like ours but not necessarily equal in length.

Others have placed long ages in a gap between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2, a view popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible, or read the days, with John Walton, as God inaugurating the world as his temple.

History cuts both ways. Most Christians through the centuries assumed a young world, and Luther and Calvin took the days as ordinary days. Yet Augustine argued that God may have made all things at once, the days being an ordering rather than ordinary days, and Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, firm defenders of the Bible’s inerrancy, accepted an old earth.

This commentary’s view

This commentary’s view: God created all things in six ordinary days. Each day is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel’s week in God’s: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11). The genealogies are true history, perhaps with small gaps, and with the six days they point to a young creation, with no ruin-and-gap before Genesis 1:2 and no death before the fall. Many faithful Christians hold an old earth, and this is not a test of salvation or of fellowship.

Holding it honestly

This view must be held honestly. It is held because of what Scripture teaches, not because the scientific evidence points that way, and its holders should say so plainly. They should not claim that the science is on their side, nor pass on weak arguments against dating methods that any geologist could take apart.

Young-earth holders reason that the distant past cannot be repeated in a laboratory, and that its reconstruction assumes that the processes we see today ran in much the same way throughout. That assumption serves well for ordinary history, but a creation week in which God spoke the world into being would not be ordinary history. It is a real argument, but difficulties remain. Light from galaxies millions of light-years away is one well-known problem, and young-earth scientists offer models that are still debated. Some appeal to a mature creation, since God made Adam a grown man and trees already bearing fruit. That has real force for a world made ready for life from the start. But Christians on every side agree that God does not deceive, and a creation that appeared to record events which never happened would raise hard questions.

So a young-earth Christian can admit, with humility, that he cannot answer every question, while trusting that God has spoken truly, and that a fuller understanding of both his books will one day show their harmony.

One church, two views

Two elders served in the same small church. One, a retired engineer, held the six-day view; the other, a geologist, held an old earth. When the young people asked about it, they answered together, each explaining his reasons and speaking warmly of the other. Then they turned to what they shared: one Creator, a good creation, humanity in God’s image, a real fall, and one Saviour.

What matters most

Whatever its age, the world exists because God spoke: “he commanded, and it stood firm” (Psalm 33:9). And the same God speaks again in the gospel. “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The God of the first day is the God of the new birth.

For reflection

Why does this commentary hold to six ordinary days and a young creation? Why is it important to admit that this view stands against the scientific consensus rather than pretend otherwise? How can Christians who differ here show that they stand on the same gospel?

4.title: Evolution and the First Adam
4.essay:
Few questions trouble thoughtful Christians more than evolution. It deserves an honest look: the science, the Christian responses, and why this commentary holds that Adam was a real man from whom all humanity descends.

What the science says

In biology, evolution is the theory that living things are related by descent from common ancestors, changing over many generations through processes such as mutation, natural selection and genetic drift. It is accepted by the overwhelming majority of biologists, including many Christians, who point to fossils, anatomy and above all genetics: patterns of shared DNA, including shared copying errors, group living things in a branching tree. Most biologists hold that humans and the great apes share common ancestors.

On human origins, most population geneticists conclude from the genetic variety in people today that our ancestors did not pass through a bottleneck of a single couple, at least within the last several hundred thousand years. A few scientists argue that a first couple remains possible further back. Others point out that a couple living much more recently could be among the genealogical ancestors of everyone alive today.

Science and philosophy

Evolution as a biological theory describes how living things change over time. Naturalism is a philosophy: the belief that nature is all there is, so that the process must be unguided and without purpose. That belief is not a finding of biology; no instrument detects the absence of God.

Charles Hodge objected to Darwinism in 1874 chiefly because it denied design. When biologists call mutations random, they mean that they do not arise in response to an organism’s needs, not that they fall outside God’s rule. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

How Christians respond

Young-earth creationists hold that God made the kinds of living things directly in the creation week, with much variation since. Old-earth creationists accept long ages but hold that God acted directly at key points, above all in creating humanity. Advocates of intelligent design argue that some features of living things are better explained by design than by unguided processes; most biologists are not persuaded, and Christians differ over its value.

Evolutionary creationists, sometimes called theistic evolutionists, believe God created all life, humans included, through evolution; many are earnest evangelicals, but they differ about Adam. Some hold that God chose a real couple from an existing population and made them the covenant head of humanity; John Stott suggested something along these lines. Others read Adam as an archetype or a symbol of every human being.

This commentary’s view

This commentary’s view: Adam and Eve were real people, specially created, from whom all humanity descends. “The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7), and made the woman from the man (Genesis 2:21–22). God “made from one man every nation of mankind” (Acts 17:26), and Luke traces Jesus’ line back to “Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). We hold this because of what Scripture teaches, knowing that it stands against the present consensus on human origins.

Why it matters

Paul builds the gospel on a comparison of two men. “Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Paul calls Adam “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14). A type is a real person whose story foreshadows another.

The argument runs from history to history: one man’s act brought condemnation, and one Man’s act brings life. All sinned in Adam, our representative head. Take away the first man and his real trespass, and the shape of Paul’s argument for the second Man is badly weakened. The same is true of the resurrection chapter: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

It matters for human dignity too. If every person on earth descends from one couple, then every nation is one family, every person bears God’s image, and no one is of a lesser kind. Christians who accept evolution and hold to a historical Adam are trying to keep Paul’s argument, and deserve a respectful hearing.

An honest answer

After a biology lecture a student asked the lecturer, a Christian, whether she had to choose between her degree and her faith. He said he held to a real Adam because of Romans 5, that the scientific questions were hard, and that he would rather live with an honest open question than give up either Christ or the truth about the evidence. Later she said his honesty helped her more than any argument.

The last Adam

“The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven… Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47, 49). Where the first Adam fell, the last Adam stood. He obeyed in our place, died for our disobedience, and rose as the firstfruits of a new humanity. In him we gain far more than we lost in Adam.

For reflection

What is the difference between evolution as a biological theory and naturalism as a philosophy? Read Romans 5:12–21: why does Paul’s argument need a real first man? How does the hope of bearing “the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49) shape the way you face hard questions?

5.title: Miracles and the Laws of Nature
5.essay:
Can a person who understands science believe in miracles? Many assume not. The answer depends on what the laws of nature are, and on who stands behind them.

What laws of nature are

The laws of nature describe how things regularly behave. They do not push the world along by themselves. In Christian understanding they describe the faithful way God ordinarily upholds his world. The Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). After the flood God promised, “While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease” (Genesis 8:22). The regularity science depends on is God keeping his word.

So a scientific explanation and God’s providence are not rivals. Rain can be described by meteorology, and Scripture says that God “prepares rain for the earth; he makes grass grow on the hills” (Psalm 147:8). Both are true. One answers the question how; the other answers who and why. God works in and through the ordinary causes he has made, and he usually works through them.

The God of the gaps

This guards us against a common mistake. If we look for God only in what science cannot yet explain, then every advance in knowledge seems to push him further out. Christian scientists such as the chemist Charles Coulson warned against this “God of the gaps”. The God of the Bible is not hiding in the gaps of our knowledge. He is the God of the whole: of what we understand as much as of what we do not. Explaining how a rainbow forms does not make it any less his sign.

Hume’s objection

The most famous argument against miracles comes from the Scottish philosopher David Hume, writing in 1748. He argued, roughly, that a miracle would break the laws of nature, that those laws rest on firm and unvarying human experience, and so that testimony to a miracle can never outweigh the evidence against it. The argument has real force against credulity, and Christians should be no more gullible than anyone else. “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

But the argument assumes too much. If experience is counted as uniform only because every report of a miracle has been ruled out in advance, it assumes what it sets out to prove. And the deeper question comes first: is there a God? If the world is upheld moment by moment by a personal Creator, he is free to act in an unusual way for his own purposes. C. S. Lewis made the point that the laws of nature tell us what will happen if nothing interferes; they cannot tell us whether God will act. When he does, the new event enters the ordinary stream of causes, and nature carries on from there. Water made wine at Cana went on to behave like wine.

Miracles are signs

Biblical miracles are not random interruptions. They cluster at great turning points: the exodus, the ministries of Elijah and Elisha, and above all the coming of Christ and the founding of his church. John calls Jesus’ miracles signs. “This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory” (John 2:11). They point beyond themselves to who he is: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41).

Miracles actually depend on the regularity of nature. We recognise them only because the world usually runs in an orderly way. The disciples knew perfectly well that the dead stay dead; that is why the empty tomb astonished them. A world of constant marvels would have no miracles at all, only chaos.

The central miracle

At the heart of Christianity stands one miracle: God raised Jesus from the dead. “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). God has given assurance of the coming judgment “to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31). The study Apologetics sets out the historical evidence. Here the point is that the resurrection is not a breach in a closed machine but the first piece of a new creation. The risen Christ said, “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see” (Luke 24:39). His body is the pattern of ours. The God who holds the laws of nature steady will one day make all things new.

Prayer and medicine

God still answers prayer, and he sometimes heals, but not always, and no one today can heal at will. Christians therefore use medicine with thanks and pray with confidence, and see no contradiction between them. Both are God’s gifts. Seeing a doctor is no failure of faith.

A surgeon prays before each operation. She gives thanks when patients recover through skill, good care and the body’s own healing, which she counts as God’s ordinary kindness. Once or twice she has seen a recovery her colleagues could not explain. She neither builds her faith on those moments nor dismisses them. She praises God for both the ordinary and the extraordinary.

For reflection

How does seeing the laws of nature as God’s faithfulness change the question of miracles? What is wrong with a “God of the gaps”? How would you answer Hume’s argument in your own words? Why is the resurrection more than a breach of natural law?

6.title: The Limits of Science, and Honest Conversations
6.essay:
Science is one of God’s good gifts. But it cannot do everything, and those who expect it to answer every question are asking more of it than it can give.

Science and scientism

Scientism is the belief that science is the only path to real knowledge, so that whatever science cannot show is mere opinion. It sounds rigorous, but it undermines itself, because that belief is not a scientific finding. No experiment could ever establish it.

Science also rests on things it cannot prove by its own methods: that our minds can be trusted to reason truly, that nature behaves consistently, and that honesty in reporting results matters. And there are questions it cannot reach. Why is there anything at all? What is good and evil? Does my life have meaning? Should this experiment be done? God “has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11), and science cannot satisfy that longing. Many scientists, believers or not, gladly admit these limits.

Fine-tuning, stated carefully

The study Apologetics introduces the argument from fine-tuning. Stated carefully: physicists have found that several constants of nature and features of the early universe, such as the relative strengths of the basic forces and the value of the cosmological constant, seem to lie within narrow ranges that allow stable stars, complex chemistry and life. Had some of them been only slightly different, as far as we can tell, no living thing could exist. This is widely acknowledged by physicists of all beliefs.

What it means is disputed. Some hope a deeper theory will show the values could not have been otherwise. Some propose a vast multiverse, in which ours is one of countless universes and we find ourselves in a life-permitting one because only such a universe could contain observers; this is speculative, but some leading physicists take it seriously. Others question whether we can assign probabilities to constants at all. Christians see design as the most natural explanation: the universe looks set up for life because it was. God “did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!” (Isaiah 45:18). The argument does not prove the God of the Bible, and should not be pressed beyond its strength. And even if a deeper law explained the constants, we could still ask why there is such a law, and why it permits life.

Talking with a scientific friend

Begin with respect. Ask questions and listen. “Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Admit what you do not know, and never use an argument you have not checked. A bad argument tells a sceptic that Christians do not care about truth.

The heart of the faith is not the age of the earth but who Jesus is and whether he rose. Show that Christianity welcomes evidence: Paul told a Roman governor that he was “speaking true and rational words” (Acts 26:25), and that “this has not been done in a corner” (Acts 26:26). And let your friend see that you delight in the world God made.

When a young person is losing faith

Some young people leave the faith over these questions because they were told, or assumed, that everything hangs on one point; when it is shaken, everything seems to fall. Do not panic, and do not shame them. Listen first: sometimes the deepest question is not about science at all. Keep Christ and his resurrection at the centre. This commentary holds to six days and a young creation, but it does not make that view a test of salvation, and a young person needs to hear that clearly. Introduce them to Christians in the sciences, pray, and be patient. “And have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 22). The study Doubt & Faith offers more help.

If doubt comes with deep despair, or with thoughts of harming yourself, please tell someone you trust today, and if you are in danger, call the emergency services or a crisis line at once. If low mood lingers, see a doctor; seeking medical help is no failure of faith.

A sixteen-year-old told his father after a biology class that he no longer believed. His father resisted the urge to argue and asked what he had learned. He admitted he knew little genetics, and they looked into the questions together, along with the evidence for the resurrection. Months later the boy said that what kept him listening was not any single answer, but that his father had not been afraid of the questions.

The wonder that remains

“When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:3–4). The answer is found in Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The God who made the stars came among us, and the One who holds all things together was nailed to a cross and rose again. That is a wonder no telescope could discover, and no discovery will ever outgrow.

For reflection

Why is scientism self-defeating? What does the fine-tuning of the universe suggest, and what does it not prove? Who do you know who is wrestling with questions of faith and science, and how could you listen to them well? How does Psalm 8 lead you from wonder at creation to worship of Christ?
